items.title: A garbage collector for LLM context windows, written in Rust
items.summary: Hi HN, Like many of you, I spend a lot of time coding with Codex and switching between cloud and local models. As a software engineer, something I never understood, and honestly hated—was `/compact` and the way it’s designed. On local models my GPU screams, and after a few hours prefill takes 2 to 3 minutes per turn. On cloud models, as the context grows, the model starts getting noticeably dumber. IMHO the root problem is context bloat and the fact that compaction destroys the quality of the model's working memory. Looking under the hood and studying how attention works, I learned that memory in modern harnesses is basically "append-only." and attention on long context becames less effective due to the attenttion dead zone. So you end up having in the context thousands of lines of old compiler dumps and duplicate file reads sitting there rent free destroying the agent's attention. Having an LLM write a summary of your conversation and blowing away your KV-cache makes no engineering sense imho especially on local models where prompt prefill latency is critical (and on cloud models where you lose prompt-cache discounts). So I built a piece of software called *contextWatcher* (or *`cw`* for friends and family). It’s a Rust proxy that runs locally on CPU ( in less than 2ms), and gives: 1. Shadow-Deduplication: Computes BLAKE3 hashes of file reads. If the agent reads for example a file like `src/main.rs` at Turn 2, edits it at Turn 5, and reads it again at Turn 9, Turns 2 and 5 are replaced with 1-line pointer stubs. Only the latest version stays in context. 2. Surgical Tool Pruning: Truncates runaway compiler output (keeping the tool_call_id, invocation, and the panic/exit trace intact) so schemas and error context never break. 3. Tail Rule Pinning: Dynamically mirrors critical system constraints (from AGENTS.md) right above the latest user prompt, pulling them out of the middle attention dead-zone without invalidating the cached prefix. 4. Swarm Prefix Multiplexing: When multiple subagents collaborate on the same workspace, cw extracts the shared root prefix (tools, rules, system prompt) so local inference engines (llama.cpp / vLLM) only keep one copy in VRAM. 5. Cache Preservation: Operates without rewriting the stable prefix, keeping prompt caching intact. On my local dual AMD GPU (Radeon Instinct Mi50 32GB) setup with a ~28k context session, cleaning out this dead weight dropped prompt prefill from ~170 seconds down to ~1.6 seconds and unlike fuzzy compaction, ground-truth code stayed 100% intact and all unit tests passed. It's open source (MIT / Apache-2.0) and installs via a one-liner: ```curl -fsSL https://constant-labs.com/cw-install.sh | sh``` Repo: https://github.com/GionaGranchelli/context-watcher For me and my setup worked pretty well, and I am satisfied with the result I get, I am really curious to see other people testing it and giving me an honest feedback on the tool and the approach

items.title: Show HN: Interview your analysts instead of auto-generating a semantic layer
items.summary: I’ve spent the last year building context for AI analysts in the mid-market. I’ve open sourced a library from my learnings, along the same principles of the Matt Pocock skills. Principles: * Claude / Codex / Cursor etc are great data agents - you just need context to enable them to answer business questions correctly. * Much of the important context lives in analysts heads' * Context must be maintainable (short, human readable - markdown and yaml) * Added context should be load bearing, not repeat of information that is available in another source of truth - and evaluations prove the value of the context * Companies should own their own context, and must be shareable with any model * Context should be version controlled (and github works as a context store). What the library does: * Performs an interview with your analysts (context-interview skill), one domain at a time, similar to what I have done as a consultant. The interview is informed by your query logs. * The AI develops evaluation questions at the same time as building the context - and at the end of each domain interview asks you to run an evaluation with and without the context. The evaluation will actually check the results against your dashboards if you allow it. We have shown increases in accuracy from 87% to 95% by adding this context in our imaginary open-source company, Shorelane. * Provides a set of skills to use the context that follow best practices for self service analytics: * Write a plain english plan for the business user to approve * Execute the plan * Verify that the execution followed the plan, and provide a simple uncertainty score. * Enable a adversarial review of the answer if their are doubts. What you get: Context repo written in markdown and yaml after you finish the interview. We use a single github repo, divided into domains. The interview can be shared and restarted by checking in/out of github. A set of skills to share with your business team Optional: We offer a fast MCP server to serve the Github-based context to your team.

Show HN: Pando, what to do with vibe coded apps at work
items.summary: Since AI has grown in popularity, technical and non-technical employees have been using it to build small tools and apps to boost productivity and model prototypes. Some companies like Ramp and Stripe, are building their own internal platform for this. That’s great for them, but not every company can, or has the bandwidth to do that. Pando is a similar idea, but fully open-source. It provides a home for these apps and tools that people build, so they get put in a centralized place with a clear owner. Apps are automatically put behind company SSO, scanned for vulnerabilities, isolated, and easily shareable. You can also put egress controls on them, and control how many apps people can deploy. Since it’s API first, there is a native CLI and MCP for it, that makes deploying super easy. Curious if this is something you are running into at your company, and if Pando sounds interesting to you! And if it doesn’t, why not?
